{{short description|Formal power series with coefficients tending to 0}}

In [[algebra]], the '''ring of restricted power series''' is the [[subring]] of a [[formal power series ring]] that consists of power series whose coefficients approach zero as degree goes to infinity.<ref name="Def">{{Citation | title=Stacks Project, Tag 0AKZ | url=http://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0AKZ}}.</ref> Over a non-archimedean [[complete field]], the [[ring (mathematics)|ring]] is also called a '''Tate algebra'''. [[Quotient ring]]s of the ring are used in the study of a [[formal algebraic space]] as well as [[rigid analysis]], the latter over non-archimedean complete fields.

Over a [[discrete topology|discrete]] [[topological ring]], the ring of restricted power series coincides with a [[polynomial ring]]; thus, in this sense, the notion of "restricted power series" is a generalization of a [[polynomial]].

== Definition ==
Let ''A'' be a [[linearly topologized ring]], separated and complete and <math>\{ I_{\lambda} \}</math> the fundamental system of open ideals. Then the ring of restricted power series is defined as the [[projective limit]] of the polynomial rings over <math>A/I_{\lambda}</math>:
:<math>A \langle x_1, \dots, x_n \rangle = \varprojlim_{\lambda} A/I_{\lambda}[x_1, \dots, x_n]</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Grothendieck|Dieudonné|1960|loc=Ch. 0, § 7.5.1.}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Bourbaki|2006|loc=Ch. III, § 4. Definition 2 and Proposition 3.}}</ref>
In other words, it is the [[completion (ring theory)|completion]] of the polynomial ring <math>A[x_1, \dots, x_n]</math> with respect to the filtration <math>\{ I_{\lambda}[x_1, \dots, x_n] \}</math>. Sometimes this ring of restricted power series is also denoted by <math>A \{ x_1, \dots, x_n \}</math>.

Clearly, the ring <math>A \langle x_1, \dots, x_n \rangle</math> can be identified with the subring of the formal power series ring <math>A[[x_1, \dots, x_n]]</math> that consists of series <math>\sum c_{\alpha} x^{\alpha}</math> with coefficients <math>c_{\alpha} \to 0</math>; i.e., each <math>I_\lambda</math> contains all but finitely many coefficients <math>c_{\alpha}</math>.
Also, the ring satisfies (and in fact is characterized by) the [[universal property]]:<ref>{{harvnb|Grothendieck|Dieudonné|1960|loc=Ch. 0, § 7.5.3.}}</ref> for (1) each [[continuous function (topology)|continuous]] [[ring homomorphism]] <math>A \to B</math> to a linearly topologized ring <math>B</math>, separated and complete and (2) each elements <math>b_1, \dots, b_n</math> in <math>B</math>, there exists a unique continuous ring homomorphism
:<math>A \langle x_1, \dots, x_n \rangle \to B, \, x_i \mapsto b_i</math>
extending <math>A \to B</math>.

== Tate algebra ==
In [[rigid analysis]], when the base ring ''A'' is the [[valuation ring]] of a complete non-archimedean field <math>(K, | \cdot |)</math>, the ring of restricted power series tensored with <math>K</math>,
:<math>T_n = K \langle \xi_1, \dots \xi_n \rangle = A \langle \xi_1, \dots, \xi_n \rangle \otimes_A K</math>
is called a Tate algebra, named for [[John Tate (mathematician)|John Tate]].<ref>{{harvnb|Fujiwara|Kato|2018|loc=Ch 0, just after Proposition 9.3.}}</ref> It is equivalently the subring of formal power series <math>k[[\xi_1, \dots, \xi_n]]</math> which consists of series convergent on <math>\mathfrak{o}_{\overline{k}}^n</math>, where <math>\mathfrak{o}_{\overline{k}} := \{x \in \overline{k} : |x| \leq 1\}</math> is the valuation ring in the [[algebraic closure]] <math>\overline{k}</math>.

The [[Glossary of commutative algebra#S|maximal spectrum]] of <math>T_n</math> is then a [[rigid-analytic space]] that models an affine space in [[rigid geometry]].

Define the '''Gauss norm''' of <math>f = \sum a_{\alpha} \xi^{\alpha} </math> in <math>T_n</math> by
:<math>\|f\| = \max_{\alpha} |a_\alpha|.</math>
This makes <math>T_n</math> a [[Banach algebra]] over ''k''; i.e., a [[normed algebra]] that is [[complete metric space|complete]] as a [[metric space]]. With this [[Norm (mathematics)|norm]], any [[Ideal (ring theory)|ideal]] <math>I</math> of <math>T_n</math> is closed<ref>{{harvnb|Bosch|2014|loc=§ 2.3. Corollary 8}}</ref> and thus, if ''I'' is radical, the quotient <math>T_n/I</math> is also a (reduced) Banach algebra called an [[affinoid algebra]].<!-- <math>T_n/I</math> is a [[Field_extension#Extension_field|finite]] [[field extension]] of the ground field <math>k</math>.-->

Some key results are:
*(Weierstrass division) Let <math>g \in T_n</math> be a <math>\xi_n</math>-distinguished series of order ''s''; i.e., <math>g = \sum_{\nu = 0}^{\infty} g_{\nu} \xi_n^{\nu}</math> where <math>g_{\nu} \in T_{n-1}</math>, <math>g_s</math> is a unit element and <math>| g_s | = \|g\| > |g_v |</math> for <math>\nu > s</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Bosch|2014|loc=§ 2.2. Definition 6.}}</ref> Then for each <math>f \in T_n</math>, there exist a unique <math>q \in T_n</math> and a unique polynomial <math>r \in T_{n-1}[\xi_n]</math> of [[degree of a polynomial|degree]] <math>< s</math> such that
*:<math>f = qg + r.</math><ref>{{harvnb|Bosch|2014|loc=§ 2.2. Theorem 8.}}</ref>
*([[Weierstrass preparation theorem|Weierstrass preparation]]) As above, let <math>g</math> be a <math>\xi_n</math>-distinguished series of order ''s''. Then there exist a unique [[monic polynomial]] <math>f \in T_{n-1}[\xi_n]</math> of degree <math>s</math> and a unit element <math>u \in T_n</math> such that <math>g = f u</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Bosch|2014|loc=§ 2.2. Corollary 9.}}</ref>
*(Noether normalization) If <math>\mathfrak{a} \subset T_n</math> is an ideal, then there is a finite homomorphism <math>T_d \hookrightarrow T_n/\mathfrak{a}</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Bosch|2014|loc=§ 2.2. Corollary 11.}}</ref>

As consequence of the division, preparation theorems and Noether normalization, <math>T_n</math> is a [[Noetherian ring|Noetherian]] [[unique factorization domain]] of [[Krull dimension]] ''n''.<ref>{{harvnb|Bosch|2014|loc=§ 2.2. Proposition 14, Proposition 15, Proposition 17.}}</ref> An analog of [[Hilbert's Nullstellensatz]] is valid: the radical of an ideal is the [[intersection (set theory)|intersection]] of all [[maximal ideal]]s containing the ideal (we say the ring is Jacobson).<ref>{{harvnb|Bosch|2014|loc=§ 2.2. Proposition 16.}}</ref>

== Results ==
{{expand section|date=April 2020}}
Results for polynomial rings such as [[Hensel's lemma]], division algorithms (or the theory of [[Gröbner bases]]) are also true for the ring of restricted power series. Throughout the section, let ''A'' denote a linearly topologized ring, separated and complete.

*(Hensel) Let <math>\mathfrak m \subset A</math> be a maximal ideal and <math>\varphi : A \to k := A/\mathfrak{m}</math> the quotient map. Given an <math>F</math> in <math>A\langle \xi \rangle</math>, if <math>\varphi(F) = gh</math> for some monic polynomial <math>g \in k[\xi]</math> and a restricted power series <math>h \in k\langle \xi \rangle</math> such that <math>g, h</math> generate the [[unit ideal]] of <math>k \langle \xi \rangle</math>, then there exist <math>G</math> in <math>A[\xi]</math> and <math>H</math> in <math>A\langle \xi \rangle</math> such that
*:<math>F = G H, \, \varphi(G) = g, \varphi(H) = h</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Bourbaki|2006|loc=Ch. III, § 4. Theorem 1.}}</ref>
